Patroclus. The childhood companion and closest friend to Achilles, he fought alongside the greatest Greek warrior at Troy. The two had been raised together, and Patroclus served as the one person who could mediate between Achilles and Agamemnon during their bitter feud. When Achilles refused to fight after his quarrel with Agamemnon, it was Patroclus who decided to take action. He donned Achilles' armor and took his place on the battlefield to inspire the flagging Greek forces and turn back the Trojan advance. Yet wearing Achilles' armor made him a target for the mightiest Trojan warrior. Hector met him in single combat and slew him, not knowing at first whose blood he had spilled. When Achilles learned of his companion's death, his grief shattered him. He wept for his lost friend and burned with a rage more intense than anything he had felt before. This grief-fueled vengeance drove Achilles back to war with a fury that transformed the entire conflict. The Iliad portrays the bond between Achilles and Patroclus as the deepest emotional connection in all the epic, the one relationship that could move Achilles' heart. Later Greek writers increasingly emphasized the romantic nature of their bond, seeing in their love the model of devoted companionship.
